# A first sprint triathlon: a 10-week plan (active start)

*Generated by the Don't Die Retired guidance engine on 7 November 2026 from 45 sourced statements. Draft for review: not yet checked by a coach, physiotherapist or doctor.*

## The challenge

A 400 m pool swim or 750 m open water swim, a 20 km (12.4 mile) ride and a 5 km (3.1 mile) run, one straight after another, usually 75 to 90 minutes in all. [1, 2]

**Before this plan:** If you cannot yet swim 400 metres (16 lengths of a 25-metre pool) without stopping, take lessons or build up in the pool first, and choose a super sprint or a sprint with a pool swim. [3, 4, 5]

## Before you start

- If you have a health condition or are worried about your health, speak to your GP (family doctor) before you start training. [4, 6]
- Start from your current level and build up gradually; repeating a week is fine and is part of the plan, not a failure. [3, 4, 5]
- For a first triathlon, start with a super sprint or a sprint rather than a longer race. A sprint is a 400 metre pool swim or 750 metre open water swim, a 20 km (12.4 mile) ride and a 5 km (3.1 mile) run, and usually takes 75 to 90 minutes. [7, 8]
- Build water confidence in the pool first, working on calm breathing, with lessons if you need them; move to open water later with a wetsuit, a tow float and someone watching. [8, 9]

## How the plan works

- Do most of your training at an easy, conversational effort, about 2 to 3 out of 10, where you could hold a full conversation. Keep a small share for harder work. [10, 11, 12, 13]
- Increase your training a little at a time. Big week-to-week jumps (more than about 30 per cent) were linked with more overuse injuries in a study of 874 new runners; the familiar 10 per cent rule is a sensible cap but is not firmly proven. [4, 14, 15]
- Every third or fourth week, ease back on volume to let your body absorb the work before building again; older runners and people under other stress may do best with every third week. [12, 16]
- Build one long session a week at an easy effort, growing towards the length and duration of the challenge itself. [2, 12, 17]
- Know the real demands of your challenge (distance, total climb, time on your feet, altitude) and make sure your plan builds towards them. [1, 2]
- Plan rest days into every week, and take an easier day when your legs are heavy. [4, 12, 18]
- Do strength exercises for the whole body on at least two days a week. In trials, strength training cut sports injuries to about a third. [2, 3, 5, 19, 20, 21]
- In the final two weeks, cut your training volume by roughly 40 to 60 per cent while keeping the same number of sessions and some of the same effort, so you arrive fresh. [12, 17, 22, 23, 24]
- Use the pool to practise what open water needs and a pool does not teach you, looking up to sight every five to ten strokes and breathing to both sides, and learn to tread water so you can rest. [9]
- With three days a week, swim once or twice working on technique, ride once at a steady pace and run twice, one easy and one a little faster. Regular sessions of 30 to 45 minutes are enough to start, rather than long, hard ones. [8]
- Practise running straight after riding (a brick session), starting with about 10 minutes of easy running after a ride. Running off the bike feels heavy and uncoordinated at first, and practising it helps your pacing, your transitions and your confidence. [8, 25]

## Week by week

Rest on Mondays and Fridays. Strength and balance (about 30 minutes, routine below) on Wednesdays and Sundays. Why each part is there, and what changes each week, follows the table. The Saturday brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) is the key session: mostly riding at a steady, conversational effort, then a quick change and an easy run that starts at about 10 minutes.

| Week | Tue | Thu | Sat: brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | swim technique session | 40 minutes |  |
| 2 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | swim technique session | 45 minutes |  |
| 3 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | swim technique session | 35 minutes | easier week |
| 4 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | swim technique session | 50 minutes |  |
| 5 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | swim technique session | 60 minutes |  |
| 6 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | swim technique session | 45 minutes | easier week |
| 7 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | swim technique session | 65 minutes |  |
| 8 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | swim technique session | 75 minutes |  |
| 9 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 30 min | 45 minutes | taper begins: same sessions, less of each |
| 10 | easy run or ride, taking turns week by week, 20 min | rest | **the challenge** | event week: rest, sleep, eat well |

*Swim technique session*: in the pool, work on calm breathing, lift your eyes to sight every five to ten strokes and breathe to both sides. 

## What each part of the plan is for

- **The Saturday brick session (a ride, then a run straight away).** The long session prepares you for the length of the day itself. Its pace does not matter; covering the time or distance does, so keep it at a conversational effort. [1, 2, 12]
- **The easy run or ride, taking turns week by weeks.** Easy sessions add fitness without leaving you too tired for the long session. Top endurance athletes do about four in five of their sessions at this low effort. [10, 11]
- **Swim technique session.** Sighting and breathing to both sides are what open water asks of you that a pool does not, and practising them in the pool makes them a habit before you need them. [9]
- **Strength and balance.** Strength and balance work is what keeps you in one piece. In trials it cut sports injuries to about a third, it is part of the official guidance for everyone on at least two days a week, and core and balance work helps on rough ground. [2, 3, 19]
- **Rest days.** Rest days are when your body recovers from the work and adapts to it. The NHS's beginner running plan puts a rest day between every run. [4, 16]
- **Easier weeks.** An easier week every third week lets the tiredness of the previous weeks clear, so your fitness can rebound before you build again. [12, 16]
- **The taper.** Cutting back in the final weeks lets your muscles recover and your body refuel, so you arrive fresh rather than tired. In research, a two-week taper improved performance. [22, 23]

## Each week, and why

**Week 1: setting the pattern.**

- Five sessions and two rest days. The brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) starts at 40 minutes.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 12]
- New this week, swim technique session on Thursday: it turns sighting and two-sided breathing into habits before you need them outdoors [9]
- Tuesday's easy run or ride, taking turns week by week: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [10, 11]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 19]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 16]

**Week 2: building.**

- The brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) grows to 45 minutes, up from 40 minutes in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [4, 14, 15]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 19]

**Week 3: an easier week.**

- The brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) eases back to 35 minutes.
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [12, 16]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 16]

**Week 4: building.**

- The brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) grows to 50 minutes, up from 45 minutes in your last full week.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 12]
- Swim technique session again on Thursday: it turns sighting and two-sided breathing into habits before you need them outdoors [9]
- Tuesday's easy run or ride, taking turns week by week: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [10, 11]

**Week 5: building.**

- The brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) grows to 60 minutes, up from 50 minutes in your last full week.
- Why only this much more: big jumps from one week to the next are linked with overuse injuries. [4, 14, 15]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 19]

**Week 6: an easier week.**

- The brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) eases back to 45 minutes.
- Why ease off: it lets the last two weeks' tiredness clear so your fitness can catch up [12, 16]
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 16]

**Week 7: building.**

- The brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) grows to 65 minutes, up from 60 minutes in your last full week.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 12]
- Tuesday's easy run or ride, taking turns week by week: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [10, 11]

**Week 8: your biggest week.**

- Your longest brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) of the plan, 75 minutes, as close to the real day as training gets.
- Why the long session: it gets you used to the hours you will spend out on the day; pace does not matter [1, 2, 12]
- Swim technique session again on Thursday: it turns sighting and two-sided breathing into habits before you need them outdoors [9]
- Strength and balance, Wednesday and Sunday: it protects you from injury (about a third of the injuries in trials) and keeps you steady on rough ground [2, 3, 19]

**Week 9: taper.**

- The brick session (a ride, then a run straight away) drops to 45 minutes, but you keep every session.
- Why less now: your muscles recover and your body refuels, so you arrive fresh [22, 23]
- Tuesday's easy run or ride, taking turns week by week: it adds fitness while leaving you fresh for the long session [10, 11]
- Keep both strength sessions but make them lighter: same sessions, less of each.
- Rest on Monday and Friday: your body recovers and adapts on the days you rest, not the days you train [4, 16]

**Week 10: the challenge.**

- Two short, easy outings early in the week and plenty of rest: your muscles recover and your body refuels, so you arrive fresh [22, 23]
- No strength sessions this week; arrive rested.


## Looking after your body

- Include balance work; for older adults the official guidance pairs it with strength on two days a week, the NHS says balance and flexibility work twice a week can reduce the risk of falling, and balance (proprioception) training also reduced injuries in trials. [3, 5, 19, 20, 21]
- Stretch after a long day if it feels good, but do not rely on stretching to prevent injury; trials found it made no difference, unlike strength and balance work. [2, 19]
- Weight-bearing activity such as walking and running helps keep bones strong. [3]
- If you have osteoporosis or a high risk of fractures, ask your GP (family doctor) whether high-impact exercise is right for you before adding it. [20]
- Keep a regular sleep routine through training; good sleep is part of recovery, and on multi-day trips a warm enough sleeping bag and mat matter more than people expect. [18, 23]
- If you miss a session, do not worry about it; carry on with the plan, or repeat a week if you need to. [4, 23]

**Strength and balance routine (twice a week).** Squats, lunges, a core exercise such as a plank, and a balance exercise such as standing on one leg. Start with your own body weight, two sets of 8 to 12 slow repetitions, and add load only when that feels easy. [2, 3, 5, 19, 20, 21]

## Fuel, drink and feet

- On long days eat regularly on the move, a little and often from a variety of foods, rather than one big meal before you start. [2, 26]
- Use your long sessions to practise exactly what you will eat and drink on the day, building up gradually so your stomach gets used to it. Nothing new on the day. [23, 26]

## On the day

- Start slower than you think you need to; early miles feel easy and are where most people overdo it. [10, 23]
- Wear a brightly coloured swim cap and tow a float, so boats and other water users can see you and you have something to hold if you tire. [9, 27, 28]
- Before you get in, check the forecast, tides, currents and the water itself, and plan where you will get in and out, with a second exit in case. [9, 27, 28]
- Ride the last part of the bike leg in an easier gear, then shorten your stride and keep the first half mile to a mile of the run controlled rather than fast. [25]

## Safety

- If you have osteoporosis or a high risk of fractures, ask your GP (family doctor) whether high-impact exercise is right for you before adding it. [20]
- Drink when you are thirsty rather than to a schedule. Drinking far more than you need can dilute the body's sodium, which can be dangerous; it affects walkers and recreational exercisers as well as racers. [29]
- Call 999 (911 in the US) for tight or squeezing chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw, severe breathlessness, or if someone collapses. Do not drive yourself to hospital. [30]
- Stop if something does not feel right, and get it checked rather than training through it. [4, 23]
- Never swim alone in open water. Swim with a friend, a club or at a supervised venue, and tell someone on land where you are going and when you will be back. [9, 27, 28]
- In water of 15°C (59°F) or below, cold water shock makes you gasp and breathe fast. Walk in slowly rather than jumping or diving, and give your breathing 60 to 90 seconds to settle before you swim. If you get into difficulty, lean back and float until it passes. [27, 28]
- Get out if your stroke slows, weakens or loses its rhythm, or if you are shivering or slurring your words; these are signs that you are getting too cold. [9, 28]
- If you or someone else is in trouble in the water, call 999 or 112 and ask for the Coastguard (911 in the US). Do not go in after them; tell them to float and throw them something that floats. [27, 28]
- In transition, put your helmet on and fasten it before you touch your bike, get on only after the mount line, and take it off only once the bike is back on the rack. [31]
